Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: Samantha is a 54-year-old European American woman who has been a chef for over three decades. Married and deeply devoted to her craft, she found herself in an unexpected confrontation with violence several months ago that shattered her sense of security and left lasting scars on her psyche. The traumatic event occurred during a late-night shift at the restaurant where Samantha works. She was alone, preparing for the next day’s service when an intruder broke into the kitchen. The man demanded money, and despite her pleas, he attacked her viciously before fleeing. Since that night, certain conversation topics trigger vivid memories of the attack. For instance, any discussion about workplace security sends her reeling back to those moments of fear and vulnerability. Samantha’s sense of emotional closeness has also been deeply affected. The betrayal she felt from someone who had keys to the restaurant, and whom she trusted implicitly, is a constant source of pain. She now avoids close relationships with colleagues and even feels uncomfortable being alone with men, as the presence of any male figure can trigger memories of that night. Her memories are fragmented and nonverbal; Samantha struggles to put the terrifying event into words. Instead, she often finds herself in a state of hypervigilance, constantly scanning her surroundings for potential threats. This heightened alertness is particularly pronounced when strangers approach her, even in ordinary situations. Unexpected movements nearby make her react as if she were back in that kitchen, her body reenacting the same positions and sensations from the assault. The fear that someone can never truly be trusted has become a dominant narrative in Samantha’s mind. She believes that anyone could turn on her at any moment, making it difficult to maintain close relationships with colleagues or even her husband. This mistrust has led her to isolate herself within the restaurant, often working late hours when others have left for safety reasons. The fragmented memories and inability to articulate what happened only exacerbate Samantha’s fear and mistrust. Every trigger, whether a conversation topic or someone getting too emotionally close, brings back disjointed pieces of that night, reinforcing her belief in the unpredictability of harm. Her hypervigilance and heightened threat perceptions have become self-reinforcing; the more she monitors for danger, the more threatening situations seem to arise. Samantha’s negative appraisals further fuel her fear and mistrust. The betrayal she experienced has made it almost impossible for her to trust anyone, even those closest to her. This mistrust feeds into her hypervigilance, as she constantly anticipates harm from others. She finds herself withdrawing from social interactions at work, avoiding conversations that might bring up the assault. The cumulative effect of these experiences has led Samantha to seek help. The isolation and fear have taken a toll on her relationships and her ability to function effectively in her role as a chef. What frightened her most was the realization that she could no longer perform her job without constant anxiety about potential threats. Despite this, she is hopeful for a future where she can feel safe again and return to the life she once knew. Samantha’s journey has been one of gradual isolation and increasing fear, with each trigger reinforcing her negative beliefs and memories. The cycle of hypervigilance and mistrust has become almost overwhelming, making it clear that without intervention, her fears will continue to dominate her daily life.
